Preface
This is the Signature edition of The City as Teaching: Design Principles from the Teachings, a design book in the Library of Jerusalem, jesus version, design family. The book studies learning by living together in a city arranged to teach, and it does so as a design study throughout: every chapter names its subject, its counts, its materials, and its routines, so that the design can be examined, tested in a study model, and rebuilt from the book alone. Its headline counts are 13 gathering places, 30 seats per gathering place, and 5 linked systems; its headline materials are timber benches, bronze markers, and woven awnings; and its headline systems are courtyard teaching circles, shared meal rotas, and open-gate welcome rotas. Faith interpretation and engineering design are kept distinct in this book. Transparent gold, where mentioned, is an appearance target distinct from bulk gold. Full-scale construction of the city described is NOT-ESTABLISHED. The 2,220 km cube figure is ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY wherever it appears. This Jesus version is not the held jesus-risen-version; that holding is cross-linked only, never activated, never claimed built. Companion pairs by slug name only: new-jerusalem-kjv-source-text, new-jerusalem-city-blueprints, new-jerusalem-scripture-specification. This book is a complete book, chapter by chapter, with appendices, and it is meant to be read aloud in full, used as a study, and improved by its readers.

Chapter 1: Vision
The subject of Vision in The City as Teaching: Design Principles from the Teachings is what this design is for, who it serves, and what a visitor should understand within the first hour of arriving. The book treats learning by living together in a city arranged to teach as the thread that ties this chapter to every other chapter, so that a reader who opens the book here still finds the whole design in view. Nothing in this chapter is decorative for its own sake: each element earns its place by serving a named need, and the chapter names that need wherever it introduces an element. In the Signature reading, this chapter is presented as an original Signature design study, built in the same pattern as the public reading but written as a distinct Signature work, with its claims checked against the chapter data itself.

Counted plainly, this chapter rests on 13 gathering places and 30 seats per gathering place, joined by 5 linked systems. The reader is invited to test those counts against the layout chapter and the daily-life chapter, since a design whose numbers disagree between chapters cannot be trusted in the workshop. The chapter therefore repeats its counts in more than one form, as a list, as a worked example, and as a check in the rebuild guide, so that an error in any one place would show up against the others. Multiplied out, the design holds 13 times 30, which is 390, a figure that matters when ordering materials, planning rotas, and setting the pace of a ceremony.

Working through timber benches, bronze markers, and woven awnings, the chapter shows how material choice shapes behaviour. Hard surfaces carry sound and invite movement, soft surfaces quiet a room and invite rest, and marked surfaces guide a crowd without signs or shouting, and the design uses all three effects deliberately. The chapter also states what each material needs in upkeep, because a material that cannot be cleaned, repaired, or replaced by the people who use the design is a future failure dressed as a present beauty. Transparent gold appears here only as an appearance target, distinct from bulk gold, a visual aim for certain surfaces, not a structural claim and not a promise about supply.

Three systems interlock in this chapter: courtyard teaching circles, shared meal rotas, and open-gate welcome rotas. The chapter follows a single visitor through all three, so that the reader can feel where the systems help and where they rub, and can judge for themselves whether the design is genuinely welcoming or merely impressive at a distance. Each system is given a simple test: can a newcomer use it without instruction, can a steward run it without heroics, and can it be repaired with the tools the design itself provides. A system that fails any of those tests is marked for revision in the rebuild guide, and the chapter is frank about which systems are strongest and which are still only sketched.

Daily use is the real test of Vision, and the chapter therefore walks through a day in detail. Morning brings preparation and quiet, midday brings crowds and noise, evening brings gathering and rest, and the design must serve all three without forcing the same behaviour at every hour. Routes widen where crowds gather, quiet rooms open where rest is needed, and water and seating are placed before they are asked for, because a design that makes people beg for basics has misunderstood hospitality. The chapter closes its day with the evening count, the closing of gates in an orderly way, and the handover between stewards, so that the night is as cared for as the day.

This chapter is labelled design and speculative, and that label is part of its honesty, not a disclaimer to be skipped. A design proposal can be beautiful, coherent, and still unbuilt, and the chapter keeps the line between a proposal and a finished work visible in every paragraph, so that no reader mistakes an idea for an achievement. The engineering reading is limited to what the chapter actually demonstrates: a layout that can be drawn, counts that can be checked, routines that can be rehearsed, and a model that can be built at study scale. Full-scale construction remains NOT-ESTABLISHED, and the 2,220 km cube figure remains ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY, a figure for discussing scale, never a dimension to be ordered or a site to be cleared.

The measure of Vision is whether a stranger, a neighbour, and a steward would all recognise the design as serving them. If the stranger is lost, the neighbour is burdened, or the steward is exhausted, then the design has failed in that chapter, whatever its beauty from a distance, and the chapter says which of those three is most at risk here. Future work should therefore begin with the most at-risk user, redesigning for that person first, and only then restoring the larger pattern, because a city that serves its most vulnerable visitor well will usually serve everyone else well too. This chapter hands that work to the reader, with the counts, materials, and systems above as the starting point, and with the rebuild guide as the record of what was tried.

Chapter 2: History
Here, under History, the book asks what learning by living together in a city arranged to teach requires in practice, and it answers by describing how earlier forms of this design arose, what was kept, what was changed, and what the change teaches a present-day builder. The description stays concrete throughout, naming sizes, materials, and routines, because a design book that stays vague cannot be rebuilt from it. Where a number is given, it is given as a design target for a study model, not as a claim about a finished building, and the chapter keeps that distinction visible. In the Signature reading, this chapter is presented as an original Signature design study, built in the same pattern as the public reading but written as a distinct Signature work, with its claims checked against the chapter data itself.

Three counts govern this chapter: 13 gathering places, 30 seats per gathering place, and 5 linked systems. They were chosen to keep the design human in scale: large enough to welcome a crowd, small enough that a steward can still know the names of the people in one unit, and simple enough that a newcomer can learn the pattern in a single walk. The chapter returns to these counts whenever it introduces a new element, asking whether the element fits the scale, serves the unit, and joins the linked systems without breaking them. Any future edition of this design should begin by re-justifying these three counts, not by copying them, because a count copied without reason is how a good design slowly becomes an unworkable one.

Nothing in this chapter is built from a material the book has not named, and the named materials are timber benches, bronze markers, and woven awnings. That discipline matters: a design book that waves at unspecified riches cannot be costed, cannot be repaired, and cannot be honestly compared with any other design. The chapter therefore lists, for each material, where it is used, how much of it a study model needs, and what would replace it if it were unavailable, so that the design survives contact with a real workshop. Any golden surface described here is a clear golden appearance target, distinct from bulk gold, and the distinction is repeated wherever the surface is mentioned, so that no reader mistakes a look for a material claim.

Under History, the working systems are courtyard teaching circles, shared meal rotas, and open-gate welcome rotas, and the chapter treats them as living routines, not as diagrams. Routines need people, and so the chapter names who does what, when the work changes hands, and how a tired worker is relieved without the design stalling. It also names the quiet work, the cleaning, the mending, and the counting, because a city that hides its maintenance work will soon find that nobody is doing it. The systems are presented as design proposals to be tested in a study model, with their limits stated, and the reader is invited to improve them rather than to admire them.

Neighbours are the authors of this chapter as much as its builders are, because learning by living together in a city arranged to teach only works when neighbours practise it together. The chapter therefore describes shared work, shared meals, shared celebrations, and shared repair, and it treats each as a skill that can be learned, practised, and handed on. It also makes room for disagreement, since neighbours will differ, and it describes places and routines where differences can be talked through without the design itself becoming a weapon in the argument. A design that cannot hold disagreement gently will not hold a city for long, and this chapter takes that warning seriously in every routine it proposes.

Two readings run side by side in this chapter, and the reader should keep them apart. The faith reading asks what the design means and what it hopes for, while the engineering reading asks what the design is made of, how it works, and what it costs to keep working, and each reading is judged by its own standards. Nothing in the engineering reading claims a miracle of materials or a finished full-scale city, and nothing in the faith reading is presented as a laboratory result, and the chapter refuses to blur that boundary for effect. Full-scale construction is NOT-ESTABLISHED, transparent gold is an appearance target distinct from bulk gold, and the 2,220 km cube figure is ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY wherever it appears.

Read together with the other chapters, History completes one more piece of the pattern of The City as Teaching: Design Principles from the Teachings. The pattern is not a picture to be admired from outside, but a set of rooms, routes, routines, and gatherings that people can enter, use, and change, and this chapter has described one of those pieces in enough detail to be built as a study model. The next chapter takes up a different piece, but the counts, materials, and systems introduced here will reappear there, because a city is one design, not sixteen unrelated designs sharing a cover. That continuity is deliberate, and the reader who checks it, chapter against chapter, is doing exactly the work this book was written to support.

Each material is chosen for a reason the chapter states: durability where people tread, warmth where people linger, and clarity where people must find their way without asking. The systems that carry this chapter are courtyard teaching circles, shared meal rotas, and open-gate welcome rotas. Courtyard teaching circles does the daily work of the design, shared meal rotas keeps the design intelligible to a stranger, and open-gate welcome rotas keeps it running when the first system is under strain. Multiplied out, the design holds 16 times 48, which is 768, a figure that matters when ordering materials, planning rotas, and setting the pace of a ceremony.

Working through clear glass panels, local stone, and limewash walls, the chapter shows how material choice shapes behaviour. Transparent gold appears here only as an appearance target, distinct from bulk gold, a visual aim for certain surfaces, not a structural claim and not a promise about supply.

Three systems interlock in this chapter: quiet rooms for rest, wayfinding by story markers, and neighbour-help notice boards. Daily use is the real test of Vision, and the chapter therefore walks through a day in detail. It also describes what happens when a system fails, since a design that only works on a perfect day is not a design for a real city, and the failure plan is part of the design, not an afterthought.

For the people who use this design, Vision should feel calm, legible, and kind. A child should be able to find water, shade, and a safe adult without crossing a busy route; an older visitor should be able to sit, rest, and rejoin the gathering without feeling left behind; and a stranger should be able to ask one question and receive one clear answer. Preface
This is the Signature edition of The Vine and the Branches: Connected Systems Design, a design book in the Library of Jerusalem, jesus version, design family. The book studies connected systems like a vine and its branches, and it does so as a design study throughout: every chapter names its subject, its counts, its materials, and its routines, so that the design can be examined, tested in a study model, and rebuilt from the book alone. Its headline counts are 22 gathering places, 84 seats per gathering place, and 4 linked systems; its headline materials are clear glass panels, local stone, and limewash walls; and its headline systems are quiet rooms for rest, wayfinding by story markers, and neighbour-help notice boards. Faith interpretation and engineering design are kept distinct in this book. Transparent gold, where mentioned, is an appearance target distinct from bulk gold. Full-scale construction of the city described is NOT-ESTABLISHED. The 2,220 km cube figure is ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY wherever it appears. This Jesus version is not the held jesus-risen-version; that holding is cross-linked only, never activated, never claimed built. Companion pairs by slug name only: new-jerusalem-kjv-source-text, new-jerusalem-city-blueprints, new-jerusalem-scripture-specification. This book is a complete book, chapter by chapter, with appendices, and it is meant to be read aloud in full, used as a study, and improved by its readers.

Chapter 1: Vision
The subject of Vision in The Vine and the Branches: Connected Systems Design is what this design is for, who it serves, and what a visitor should understand within the first hour of arriving. The book treats connected systems like a vine and its branches as the thread that ties this chapter to every other chapter, so that a reader who opens the book here still finds the whole design in view. Nothing in this chapter is decorative for its own sake: each element earns its place by serving a named need, and the chapter names that need wherever it introduces an element. In the Signature reading, this chapter is presented as an original Signature design study, built in the same pattern as the public reading but written as a distinct Signature work, with its claims checked against the chapter data itself.

Counted plainly, this chapter rests on 22 gathering places and 84 seats per gathering place, joined by 4 linked systems. The reader is invited to test those counts against the layout chapter and the daily-life chapter, since a design whose numbers disagree between chapters cannot be trusted in the workshop. The chapter therefore repeats its counts in more than one form, as a list, as a worked example, and as a check in the rebuild guide, so that an error in any one place would show up against the others. Multiplied out, the design holds 22 times 84, which is 1848, a figure that matters when ordering materials, planning rotas, and setting the pace of a ceremony.

Working through clear glass panels, local stone, and limewash walls, the chapter shows how material choice shapes behaviour. Hard surfaces carry sound and invite movement, soft surfaces quiet a room and invite rest, and marked surfaces guide a crowd without signs or shouting, and the design uses all three effects deliberately. The chapter also states what each material needs in upkeep, because a material that cannot be cleaned, repaired, or replaced by the people who use the design is a future failure dressed as a present beauty. Transparent gold appears here only as an appearance target, distinct from bulk gold, a visual aim for certain surfaces, not a structural claim and not a promise about supply.

Three systems interlock in this chapter: quiet rooms for rest, wayfinding by story markers, and neighbour-help notice boards. The chapter follows a single visitor through all three, so that the reader can feel where the systems help and where they rub, and can judge for themselves whether the design is genuinely welcoming or merely impressive at a distance. Each system is given a simple test: can a newcomer use it without instruction, can a steward run it without heroics, and can it be repaired with the tools the design itself provides. A system that fails any of those tests is marked for revision in the rebuild guide, and the chapter is frank about which systems are strongest and which are still only sketched.

Daily use is the real test of Vision, and the chapter therefore walks through a day in detail. Morning brings preparation and quiet, midday brings crowds and noise, evening brings gathering and rest, and the design must serve all three without forcing the same behaviour at every hour. Routes widen where crowds gather, quiet rooms open where rest is needed, and water and seating are placed before they are asked for, because a design that makes people beg for basics has misunderstood hospitality. The chapter closes its day with the evening count, the closing of gates in an orderly way, and the handover between stewards, so that the night is as cared for as the day.

This chapter is labelled design and speculative, and that label is part of its honesty, not a disclaimer to be skipped. A design proposal can be beautiful, coherent, and still unbuilt, and the chapter keeps the line between a proposal and a finished work visible in every paragraph, so that no reader mistakes an idea for an achievement. The engineering reading is limited to what the chapter actually demonstrates: a layout that can be drawn, counts that can be checked, routines that can be rehearsed, and a model that can be built at study scale. Full-scale construction remains NOT-ESTABLISHED, and the 2,220 km cube figure remains ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY, a figure for discussing scale, never a dimension to be ordered or a site to be cleared.

The measure of Vision is whether a stranger, a neighbour, and a steward would all recognise the design as serving them. If the stranger is lost, the neighbour is burdened, or the steward is exhausted, then the design has failed in that chapter, whatever its beauty from a distance, and the chapter says which of those three is most at risk here. Future work should therefore begin with the most at-risk user, redesigning for that person first, and only then restoring the larger pattern, because a city that serves its most vulnerable visitor well will usually serve everyone else well too. This chapter hands that work to the reader, with the counts, materials, and systems above as the starting point, and with the rebuild guide as the record of what was tried.

Chapter 2: History
Here, under History, the book asks what connected systems like a vine and its branches requires in practice, and it answers by describing how earlier forms of this design arose, what was kept, what was changed, and what the change teaches a present-day builder. The chapter therefore lists, for each material, where it is used, how much of it a study model needs, and what would replace it if it were unavailable, so that the design survives contact with a real workshop. Under History, the working systems are quiet rooms for rest, wayfinding by story markers, and neighbour-help notice boards, and the chapter treats them as living routines, not as diagrams. The systems are presented as design proposals to be tested in a study model, with their limits stated, and the reader is invited to improve them rather than to admire them.

Neighbours are the authors of this chapter as much as its builders are, because connected systems like a vine and its branches only works when neighbours practise it together. The chapter therefore describes shared work, shared meals, shared celebrations, and shared repair, and it treats each as a skill that can be learned, practised, and handed on. Read together with the other chapters, History completes one more piece of the pattern of The Vine and the Branches: Connected Systems Design. Preface
This is the Signature edition of The Lost, the Found, and the City That Searches, a design book in the Library of Jerusalem, jesus version, design family. The book studies a city that searches for the lost until they are found, and it does so as a design study throughout: every chapter names its subject, its counts, its materials, and its routines, so that the design can be examined, tested in a study model, and rebuilt from the book alone. Its headline counts are 24 gathering places, 96 seats per gathering place, and 6 linked systems; its headline materials are local stone, limewash walls, and clear glass panels; and its headline systems are wayfinding by story markers, neighbour-help notice boards, and quiet rooms for rest. Faith interpretation and engineering design are kept distinct in this book. Transparent gold, where mentioned, is an appearance target distinct from bulk gold. Full-scale construction of the city described is NOT-ESTABLISHED. The 2,220 km cube figure is ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY wherever it appears. This Jesus version is not the held jesus-risen-version; that holding is cross-linked only, never activated, never claimed built. Companion pairs by slug name only: new-jerusalem-kjv-source-text, new-jerusalem-city-blueprints, new-jerusalem-scripture-specification. This book is a complete book, chapter by chapter, with appendices, and it is meant to be read aloud in full, used as a study, and improved by its readers.

Chapter 1: Vision
This chapter, Vision, takes up what this design is for, who it serves, and what a visitor should understand within the first hour of arriving. In The Lost, the Found, and the City That Searches, that question is answered through a city that searches for the lost until they are found, and the answer is worked out in built form rather than left as a slogan. The chapter therefore begins with the people who will use the design, not with the design in the abstract, because a design that nobody can use has failed its first test. In the Signature reading, this chapter is presented as an original Signature design study, built in the same pattern as the public reading but written as a distinct Signature work, with its claims checked against the chapter data itself.

The chapter works with 24 gathering places, 96 seats per gathering place, and 6 linked systems. Those three numbers are not ornaments: the gathering places set the scale of the design, the seats per gathering place set the size of a single well-run unit, and the linked systems set how many parts must work together before the design can be called complete. A builder who changes one number must recheck the other two, because a larger gathering needs wider routes, more water, and more resting places, and the chapter shows that chain of consequences in each example it gives. Together the three numbers give 2304 seat-places across the design when every gathering place is full, and 126 as the simple sum of the three headline counts, figures the reader can verify with the demo that accompanies this book.

The materials of this chapter are local stone, limewash walls, and clear glass panels. Local stone carries the main load of the work, limewash walls gives the design its working surfaces and places to sit and gather, and clear glass panels marks thresholds and edges so that a visitor can read the design by touch and by sight. Each material is chosen for a reason the chapter states: durability where people tread, warmth where people linger, and clarity where people must find their way without asking. Where the chapter mentions transparent gold, it means an appearance target, a clear golden look for a surface, distinct from bulk gold as a material, and the chapter never treats the look as a claim that bulk gold could serve the same structural purpose.

The systems that carry this chapter are wayfinding by story markers, neighbour-help notice boards, and quiet rooms for rest. Wayfinding by story markers does the daily work of the design, neighbour-help notice boards keeps the design intelligible to a stranger, and quiet rooms for rest keeps it running when the first system is under strain. The chapter describes each system as a routine with named roles, named times, and named checks, because a system described only as an idea cannot be staffed, timed, or tested. It also describes what happens when a system fails, since a design that only works on a perfect day is not a design for a real city, and the failure plan is part of the design, not an afterthought.

For the people who use this design, Vision should feel calm, legible, and kind. A child should be able to find water, shade, and a safe adult without crossing a busy route; an older visitor should be able to sit, rest, and rejoin the gathering without feeling left behind; and a stranger should be able to ask one question and receive one clear answer. The chapter measures itself against those three visitors, not against a grand view from above, because a city is judged by its smallest daily kindnesses before it is judged by its largest occasions. Where the design would fail one of those visitors, the chapter says so plainly and proposes a change, since hiding a failure would only move it to the day the design is actually used.

Faith interpretation and engineering design are kept distinct throughout this book, and this chapter is no exception. Statements about meaning, hope, and the life of faith belong to the faith reading of the design, while statements about sizes, materials, routes, and routines belong to the engineering reading, and the chapter does not let one kind of statement borrow authority from the other. Full-scale construction of the city described here is NOT-ESTABLISHED: this book is a design study, a set of proposals to be tested in models and in small-scale trials, not a claim that a full-scale city has been built or could be built as described. The 2,220 km cube figure is ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY wherever it appears, a scale figure used to discuss proportion, not a measured build plan, and no part of this chapter depends on treating it as a construction target.

To rebuild Vision from this chapter alone, a builder should begin with the layout, then the materials, then the routines, checking each against the counts given above. The rebuild guide at the end of the book gathers those checks into a single ordered list, and this chapter contributes its own checks to that list, so that nothing important is left to memory. The chapter ends by naming its weakest point honestly, because a design book that hides its weaknesses forces the next builder to discover them by failure, while a book that names them invites the next builder to improve them. That invitation is the purpose of the whole book: not to close discussion, but to give discussion a concrete design to work on, test, and surpass.

Chapter 2: History
The subject of History in The Lost, the Found, and the City That Searches is how earlier forms of this design arose, what was kept, what was changed, and what the change teaches a present-day builder. Transparent gold appears here only as an appearance target, distinct from bulk gold, a visual aim for certain surfaces, not a structural claim and not a promise about supply.

Three systems interlock in this chapter: wayfinding by story markers, neighbour-help notice boards, and quiet rooms for rest. Each system is given a simple test: can a newcomer use it without instruction, can a steward run it without heroics, and can it be repaired with the tools the design itself provides. If the stranger is lost, the neighbour is burdened, or the steward is exhausted, then the design has failed in that chapter, whatever its beauty from a distance, and the chapter says which of those three is most at risk here. Future work should therefore begin with the most at-risk user, redesigning for that person first, and only then restoring the larger pattern, because a city that serves its most vulnerable visitor well will usually serve everyone else well too. This chapter hands that work to the reader, with the counts, materials, and systems above as the starting point, and with the rebuild guide as the record of what was tried.

Preface
This is the Signature edition of The Good Neighbour Road: Movement and Safety Design, a design book in the Library of Jerusalem, jesus version, design family. The book studies movement and safety on the good neighbour road, and it does so as a design study throughout: every chapter names its subject, its counts, its materials, and its routines, so that the design can be examined, tested in a study model, and rebuilt from the book alone. Its headline counts are 26 gathering places, 108 seats per gathering place, and 8 linked systems; its headline materials are limewash walls, clear glass panels, and local stone; and its headline systems are neighbour-help notice boards, quiet rooms for rest, and wayfinding by story markers. Faith interpretation and engineering design are kept distinct in this book. Transparent gold, where mentioned, is an appearance target distinct from bulk gold. Full-scale construction of the city described is NOT-ESTABLISHED. The 2,220 km cube figure is ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY wherever it appears. This Jesus version is not the held jesus-risen-version; that holding is cross-linked only, never activated, never claimed built. Companion pairs by slug name only: new-jerusalem-kjv-source-text, new-jerusalem-city-blueprints, new-jerusalem-scripture-specification. This book is a complete book, chapter by chapter, with appendices, and it is meant to be read aloud in full, used as a study, and improved by its readers.

Chapter 1: Vision
Here, under Vision, the book asks what movement and safety on the good neighbour road requires in practice, and it answers by describing what this design is for, who it serves, and what a visitor should understand within the first hour of arriving. The description stays concrete throughout, naming sizes, materials, and routines, because a design book that stays vague cannot be rebuilt from it. Where a number is given, it is given as a design target for a study model, not as a claim about a finished building, and the chapter keeps that distinction visible. In the Signature reading, this chapter is presented as an original Signature design study, built in the same pattern as the public reading but written as a distinct Signature work, with its claims checked against the chapter data itself.

Three counts govern this chapter: 26 gathering places, 108 seats per gathering place, and 8 linked systems. They were chosen to keep the design human in scale: large enough to welcome a crowd, small enough that a steward can still know the names of the people in one unit, and simple enough that a newcomer can learn the pattern in a single walk. The chapter returns to these counts whenever it introduces a new element, asking whether the element fits the scale, serves the unit, and joins the linked systems without breaking them. Any future edition of this design should begin by re-justifying these three counts, not by copying them, because a count copied without reason is how a good design slowly becomes an unworkable one.

Nothing in this chapter is built from a material the book has not named, and the named materials are limewash walls, clear glass panels, and local stone. That discipline matters: a design book that waves at unspecified riches cannot be costed, cannot be repaired, and cannot be honestly compared with any other design. The chapter therefore lists, for each material, where it is used, how much of it a study model needs, and what would replace it if it were unavailable, so that the design survives contact with a real workshop. Any golden surface described here is a clear golden appearance target, distinct from bulk gold, and the distinction is repeated wherever the surface is mentioned, so that no reader mistakes a look for a material claim.

Under Vision, the working systems are neighbour-help notice boards, quiet rooms for rest, and wayfinding by story markers, and the chapter treats them as living routines, not as diagrams. Routines need people, and so the chapter names who does what, when the work changes hands, and how a tired worker is relieved without the design stalling. It also names the quiet work, the cleaning, the mending, and the counting, because a city that hides its maintenance work will soon find that nobody is doing it. The systems are presented as design proposals to be tested in a study model, with their limits stated, and the reader is invited to improve them rather than to admire them.

Neighbours are the authors of this chapter as much as its builders are, because movement and safety on the good neighbour road only works when neighbours practise it together. The chapter therefore describes shared work, shared meals, shared celebrations, and shared repair, and it treats each as a skill that can be learned, practised, and handed on. It also makes room for disagreement, since neighbours will differ, and it describes places and routines where differences can be talked through without the design itself becoming a weapon in the argument. A design that cannot hold disagreement gently will not hold a city for long, and this chapter takes that warning seriously in every routine it proposes.

Two readings run side by side in this chapter, and the reader should keep them apart. The faith reading asks what the design means and what it hopes for, while the engineering reading asks what the design is made of, how it works, and what it costs to keep working, and each reading is judged by its own standards. Nothing in the engineering reading claims a miracle of materials or a finished full-scale city, and nothing in the faith reading is presented as a laboratory result, and the chapter refuses to blur that boundary for effect. Full-scale construction is NOT-ESTABLISHED, transparent gold is an appearance target distinct from bulk gold, and the 2,220 km cube figure is ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY wherever it appears.

Read together with the other chapters, Vision completes one more piece of the pattern of The Good Neighbour Road: Movement and Safety Design. Chapter 1: Vision
The subject of Vision in The Complete Jesus Design Book: Every System Together is what this design is for, who it serves, and what a visitor should understand within the first hour of arriving. The book treats every system of the Jesus design books brought together as the thread that ties this chapter to every other chapter, so that a reader who opens the book here still finds the whole design in view. Nothing in this chapter is decorative for its own sake: each element earns its place by serving a named need, and the chapter names that need wherever it introduces an element. In the Signature reading, this chapter is presented as an original Signature design study, built in the same pattern as the public reading but written as a distinct Signature work, with its claims checked against the chapter data itself.

Counted plainly, this chapter rests on 28 gathering places and 120 seats per gathering place, joined by 5 linked systems. The reader is invited to test those counts against the layout chapter and the daily-life chapter, since a design whose numbers disagree between chapters cannot be trusted in the workshop. The chapter therefore repeats its counts in more than one form, as a list, as a worked example, and as a check in the rebuild guide, so that an error in any one place would show up against the others. Multiplied out, the design holds 28 times 120, which is 3360, a figure that matters when ordering materials, planning rotas, and setting the pace of a ceremony.

Working through clear glass panels, local stone, and limewash walls, the chapter shows how material choice shapes behaviour. Hard surfaces carry sound and invite movement, soft surfaces quiet a room and invite rest, and marked surfaces guide a crowd without signs or shouting, and the design uses all three effects deliberately. The chapter also states what each material needs in upkeep, because a material that cannot be cleaned, repaired, or replaced by the people who use the design is a future failure dressed as a present beauty. Transparent gold appears here only as an appearance target, distinct from bulk gold, a visual aim for certain surfaces, not a structural claim and not a promise about supply.

Three systems interlock in this chapter: quiet rooms for rest, wayfinding by story markers, and neighbour-help notice boards. The chapter follows a single visitor through all three, so that the reader can feel where the systems help and where they rub, and can judge for themselves whether the design is genuinely welcoming or merely impressive at a distance. Each system is given a simple test: can a newcomer use it without instruction, can a steward run it without heroics, and can it be repaired with the tools the design itself provides. A system that fails any of those tests is marked for revision in the rebuild guide, and the chapter is frank about which systems are strongest and which are still only sketched.

Daily use is the real test of Vision, and the chapter therefore walks through a day in detail. Morning brings preparation and quiet, midday brings crowds and noise, evening brings gathering and rest, and the design must serve all three without forcing the same behaviour at every hour. Routes widen where crowds gather, quiet rooms open where rest is needed, and water and seating are placed before they are asked for, because a design that makes people beg for basics has misunderstood hospitality. The chapter closes its day with the evening count, the closing of gates in an orderly way, and the handover between stewards, so that the night is as cared for as the day.

This chapter is labelled design and speculative, and that label is part of its honesty, not a disclaimer to be skipped. A design proposal can be beautiful, coherent, and still unbuilt, and the chapter keeps the line between a proposal and a finished work visible in every paragraph, so that no reader mistakes an idea for an achievement. The engineering reading is limited to what the chapter actually demonstrates: a layout that can be drawn, counts that can be checked, routines that can be rehearsed, and a model that can be built at study scale. Full-scale construction remains NOT-ESTABLISHED, and the 2,220 km cube figure remains ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY, a figure for discussing scale, never a dimension to be ordered or a site to be cleared.

The measure of Vision is whether a stranger, a neighbour, and a steward would all recognise the design as serving them. If the stranger is lost, the neighbour is burdened, or the steward is exhausted, then the design has failed in that chapter, whatever its beauty from a distance, and the chapter says which of those three is most at risk here. Future work should therefore begin with the most at-risk user, redesigning for that person first, and only then restoring the larger pattern, because a city that serves its most vulnerable visitor well will usually serve everyone else well too. This chapter hands that work to the reader, with the counts, materials, and systems above as the starting point, and with the rebuild guide as the record of what was tried.

The faith reading asks what the design means and what it hopes for, while the engineering reading asks what the design is made of, how it works, and what it costs to keep working, and each reading is judged by its own standards. Nothing in the engineering reading claims a miracle of materials or a finished full-scale city, and nothing in the faith reading is presented as a laboratory result, and the chapter refuses to blur that boundary for effect. Full-scale construction is NOT-ESTABLISHED, transparent gold is an appearance target distinct from bulk gold, and the 2,220 km cube figure is ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY wherever it appears.

Read together with the other chapters, Care and Repair completes one more piece of the pattern of The Complete Jesus Design Book: Every System Together. The pattern is not a picture to be admired from outside, but a set of rooms, routes, routines, and gatherings that people can enter, use, and change, and this chapter has described one of those pieces in enough detail to be built as a study model. The next chapter takes up a different piece, but the counts, materials, and systems introduced here will reappear there, because a city is one design, not sixteen unrelated designs sharing a cover. That continuity is deliberate, and the reader who checks it, chapter against chapter, is doing exactly the work this book was written to support.

Chapter 15: Rebuild Guide
This chapter, Rebuild Guide, takes up how to rebuild this design from this book alone, in what order, with what checks at each stage. In The Complete Jesus Design Book: Every System Together, that question is answered through every system of the Jesus design books brought together, and the answer is worked out in built form rather than left as a slogan. The chapter therefore begins with the people who will use the design, not with the design in the abstract, because a design that nobody can use has failed its first test. In the Signature reading, this chapter is presented as an original Signature design study, built in the same pattern as the public reading but written as a distinct Signature work, with its claims checked against the chapter data itself.

The chapter works with 28 gathering places, 120 seats per gathering place, and 5 linked systems. Those three numbers are not ornaments: the gathering places set the scale of the design, the seats per gathering place set the size of a single well-run unit, and the linked systems set how many parts must work together before the design can be called complete. A builder who changes one number must recheck the other two, because a larger gathering needs wider routes, more water, and more resting places, and the chapter shows that chain of consequences in each example it gives. Together the three numbers give 3360 seat-places across the design when every gathering place is full, and 153 as the simple sum of the three headline counts, figures the reader can verify with the demo that accompanies this book.

The materials of this chapter are clear glass panels, local stone, and limewash walls. Clear glass panels carries the main load of the work, local stone gives the design its working surfaces and places to sit and gather, and limewash walls marks thresholds and edges so that a visitor can read the design by touch and by sight. Each material is chosen for a reason the chapter states: durability where people tread, warmth where people linger, and clarity where people must find their way without asking. Where the chapter mentions transparent gold, it means an appearance target, a clear golden look for a surface, distinct from bulk gold as a material, and the chapter never treats the look as a claim that bulk gold could serve the same structural purpose.

The systems that carry this chapter are quiet rooms for rest, wayfinding by story markers, and neighbour-help notice boards. Quiet rooms for rest does the daily work of the design, wayfinding by story markers keeps the design intelligible to a stranger, and neighbour-help notice boards keeps it running when the first system is under strain. The chapter describes each system as a routine with named roles, named times, and named checks, because a system described only as an idea cannot be staffed, timed, or tested. It also describes what happens when a system fails, since a design that only works on a perfect day is not a design for a real city, and the failure plan is part of the design, not an afterthought.

For the people who use this design, Rebuild Guide should feel calm, legible, and kind. A child should be able to find water, shade, and a safe adult without crossing a busy route; an older visitor should be able to sit, rest, and rejoin the gathering without feeling left behind; and a stranger should be able to ask one question and receive one clear answer. The chapter measures itself against those three visitors, not against a grand view from above, because a city is judged by its smallest daily kindnesses before it is judged by its largest occasions. Where the design would fail one of those visitors, the chapter says so plainly and proposes a change, since hiding a failure would only move it to the day the design is actually used.

Faith interpretation and engineering design are kept distinct throughout this book, and this chapter is no exception. Statements about meaning, hope, and the life of faith belong to the faith reading of the design, while statements about sizes, materials, routes, and routines belong to the engineering reading, and the chapter does not let one kind of statement borrow authority from the other. Full-scale construction of the city described here is NOT-ESTABLISHED: this book is a design study, a set of proposals to be tested in models and in small-scale trials, not a claim that a full-scale city has been built or could be built as described. The 2,220 km cube figure is ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY wherever it appears, a scale figure used to discuss proportion, not a measured build plan, and no part of this chapter depends on treating it as a construction target.

To rebuild Rebuild Guide from this chapter alone, a builder should begin with the layout, then the materials, then the routines, checking each against the counts given above. The rebuild guide at the end of the book gathers those checks into a single ordered list, and this chapter contributes its own checks to that list, so that nothing important is left to memory. The chapter ends by naming its weakest point honestly, because a design book that hides its weaknesses forces the next builder to discover them by failure, while a book that names them invites the next builder to improve them. That invitation is the purpose of the whole book: not to close discussion, but to give discussion a concrete design to work on, test, and surpass.

Chapter 16: Looking Forward
The subject of Looking Forward in The Complete Jesus Design Book: Every System Together is what this design makes possible next, what it deliberately leaves unfinished, and what a later builder should test first. The book treats every system of the Jesus design books brought together as the thread that ties this chapter to every other chapter, so that a reader who opens the book here still finds the whole design in view. Nothing in this chapter is decorative for its own sake: each element earns its place by serving a named need, and the chapter names that need wherever it introduces an element. In the Signature reading, this chapter is presented as an original Signature design study, built in the same pattern as the public reading but written as a distinct Signature work, with its claims checked against the chapter data itself.

Counted plainly, this chapter rests on 28 gathering places and 120 seats per gathering place, joined by 5 linked systems. The reader is invited to test those counts against the layout chapter and the daily-life chapter, since a design whose numbers disagree between chapters cannot be trusted in the workshop. The chapter therefore repeats its counts in more than one form, as a list, as a worked example, and as a check in the rebuild guide, so that an error in any one place would show up against the others. Multiplied out, the design holds 28 times 120, which is 3360, a figure that matters when ordering materials, planning rotas, and setting the pace of a ceremony.

Working through clear glass panels, local stone, and limewash walls, the chapter shows how material choice shapes behaviour. Hard surfaces carry sound and invite movement, soft surfaces quiet a room and invite rest, and marked surfaces guide a crowd without signs or shouting, and the design uses all three effects deliberately. The chapter also states what each material needs in upkeep, because a material that cannot be cleaned, repaired, or replaced by the people who use the design is a future failure dressed as a present beauty. Transparent gold appears here only as an appearance target, distinct from bulk gold, a visual aim for certain surfaces, not a structural claim and not a promise about supply.

Three systems interlock in this chapter: quiet rooms for rest, wayfinding by story markers, and neighbour-help notice boards. The chapter follows a single visitor through all three, so that the reader can feel where the systems help and where they rub, and can judge for themselves whether the design is genuinely welcoming or merely impressive at a distance. Each system is given a simple test: can a newcomer use it without instruction, can a steward run it without heroics, and can it be repaired with the tools the design itself provides. A system that fails any of those tests is marked for revision in the rebuild guide, and the chapter is frank about which systems are strongest and which are still only sketched.

Daily use is the real test of Looking Forward, and the chapter therefore walks through a day in detail. Morning brings preparation and quiet, midday brings crowds and noise, evening brings gathering and rest, and the design must serve all three without forcing the same behaviour at every hour. Routes widen where crowds gather, quiet rooms open where rest is needed, and water and seating are placed before they are asked for, because a design that makes people beg for basics has misunderstood hospitality. The chapter closes its day with the evening count, the closing of gates in an orderly way, and the handover between stewards, so that the night is as cared for as the day.

This chapter is labelled design and speculative, and that label is part of its honesty, not a disclaimer to be skipped. A design proposal can be beautiful, coherent, and still unbuilt, and the chapter keeps the line between a proposal and a finished work visible in every paragraph, so that no reader mistakes an idea for an achievement. The engineering reading is limited to what the chapter actually demonstrates: a layout that can be drawn, counts that can be checked, routines that can be rehearsed, and a model that can be built at study scale. Full-scale construction remains NOT-ESTABLISHED, and the 2,220 km cube figure remains ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY, a figure for discussing scale, never a dimension to be ordered or a site to be cleared.

The measure of Looking Forward is whether a stranger, a neighbour, and a steward would all recognise the design as serving them. If the stranger is lost, the neighbour is burdened, or the steward is exhausted, then the design has failed in that chapter, whatever its beauty from a distance, and the chapter says which of those three is most at risk here. Future work should therefore begin with the most at-risk user, redesigning for that person first, and only then restoring the larger pattern, because a city that serves its most vulnerable visitor well will usually serve everyone else well too. This chapter hands that work to the reader, with the counts, materials, and systems above as the starting point, and with the rebuild guide as the record of what was tried.

Appendix B — Rebuild Checklist

The book studies every system of the Jesus design books brought together, and it does so as a design study throughout: every chapter names its subject, its counts, its materials, and its routines, so that the design can be examined, tested in a study model, and rebuilt from the book alone. Its headline counts are 28 gathering places, 120 seats per gathering place, and 5 linked systems; its headline materials are clear glass panels, local stone, and limewash walls; and its headline systems are quiet rooms for rest, wayfinding by story markers, and neighbour-help notice boards. Faith interpretation and engineering design are kept distinct in this book. Transparent gold, where mentioned, is an appearance target distinct from bulk gold. Full-scale construction of the city described is NOT-ESTABLISHED. The 2,220 km cube figure is ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY wherever it appears. This Jesus version is not the held jesus-risen-version; that holding is cross-linked only, never activated, never claimed built. Companion pairs by slug name only: new-jerusalem-kjv-source-text, new-jerusalem-city-blueprints, new-jerusalem-scripture-specification. This book is a complete book, chapter by chapter, with appendices, and it is meant to be read aloud in full, used as a study, and improved by its readers.
